slides.title: Your app is mostly other people's code
slides.summary: A typical frontend pulls in hundreds of packages. Any one of them can be vulnerable or malicious.
body: Most of the code in a modern bundle comes from node_modules. Attacks on that supply chain take a few forms:

ul: Known vulnerabilities in an old version of a library.
Compromised maintainers: a phished or stolen npm token publishes a malicious version of a popular package.
Self-spreading worms: an install script steals tokens and uses them to infect more packages.

body: <mark>Every dependency is code you ship with full access to your page and, at install time, to your machines.</mark>

body.more: 2025: the year npm got attacked at scale
text: September 8: a phished maintainer account pushed malicious versions of chalk, debug and other packages with billions of weekly downloads. The payload ran in browsers and swapped crypto wallet addresses.

From September 14: the Shai-Hulud worm used postinstall scripts to steal npm and cloud tokens and publish infected versions of other packages; GitHub removed 500+ packages. In response npm moved publishing towards trusted publishing, short-lived tokens and mandatory 2FA.

items.label: one compromised package
items.sub: runs in users' browsers and on your CI

figure.alt: A dependency tree: your app depends on a few direct packages, which pull in many transitive packages. One transitive package, deep in the tree, is compromised. Two red paths lead out of it. Into the bundle: the code ships to users' browsers and can, for example, rewrite crypto wallet addresses or steal form data, as in the September 2025 chalk and debug compromise. Into install scripts: a postinstall script runs on developer laptops and CI, steals npm, GitHub and cloud tokens, and uses them to publish infected versions of more packages, which is how the Shai-Hulud worm spread to hundreds of packages in 2025.

slides.title: Keeping dependencies safe
slides.summary: Lock versions, delay brand-new releases, limit install scripts, audit continuously and publish with trusted publishing.

ul: Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, so CI uses exactly the reviewed versions.
Don't run install scripts you don't need. pnpm 10+ skips dependency lifecycle scripts unless you allow them; with npm, use --ignore-scripts where you can.
Wait before adopting new releases. Most malicious versions are caught within days; pnpm's minimumReleaseAge and Renovate's release-age settings enforce a delay.
Audit continuously with Dependabot, Renovate or npm audit, and update in small steps.
Use trusted publishing (OIDC from CI) instead of long-lived npm tokens, and phishing-resistant 2FA.
Publish with provenance, so users can check which repo and workflow built the package (npm audit signatures).

body.note: npm audit reports a lot of noise from dev-only tools. Triage by whether the vulnerable code ships to users or runs in CI.

code: npm ci --ignore-scripts      # exact lockfile, no install scripts
npm audit --omit=dev         # what ships to users
npm audit signatures         # verify registry signatures + provenance
minimumReleaseAge: 1440      # minutes: skip versions < 1 day old
